## Before the seminar

<!-- At home, before the seminar. -->

The lecture proved one result, the propensity weighting theorem, which you prove again with the slides closed (exercise 4). It stated the optimal threshold theorem and the adjustment theorem and left their proofs to you (exercises 1 and 3), and it stated the confounding gap without deriving it (exercise 2). Do all four on paper before the seminar; the seminar's problems are variations on them. You may use, without proof, two facts from ST102: the tower property, $\mathbb E[W] = \mathbb E\big[\mathbb E[W \mid X]\big]$, and that if $V$ is independent of $X$, then $\mathbb E[k(X, V) \mid X = x] = \mathbb E[k(x, V)]$ for any function $k$ (freeze $X$ at $x$; the distribution of $V$ does not move). Throughout, assume that every expectation that appears exists: finite means, and finite variances wherever a variance or covariance appears.

::: {.callout-warning title="Hints"}
Each exercise has hints, collapsed below it. Do not open a hint unless you have been stuck for at least a few minutes, and open them in order. Exercise 4's proof is on the lecture slides. Solutions to exercises 1 to 3 are shown in the seminar if you ask.
:::

**Exercise 1 (optimal threshold theorem).** Let $p(x) = P(Y = 1 \mid X = x)$. A false positive (predict $1$, truth $0$) costs $c_{FP} \ge 0$, a false negative (predict $0$, truth $1$) costs $c_{FN} \ge 0$, not both are $0$, and a correct prediction costs nothing. A rule $\delta$ assigns a prediction $\delta(x) \in \{0, 1\}$ to every $x$.

(a) At a fixed $x$, write the expected cost of predicting $1$ and the expected cost of predicting $0$.

(b) Show that predicting $1$ has the smaller expected cost exactly when $p(x) > c^\star = c_{FP}/(c_{FP} + c_{FN})$. What happens at $p(x) = c^\star$?

(c) Let $\delta^\star$ be the rule from (b). Show that $\mathbb E\big[\text{cost}(\delta^\star(X), Y)\big] \le \mathbb E\big[\text{cost}(\delta(X), Y)\big]$ for every rule $\delta$.

(d) With equal costs, what is $c^\star$, and what is the probability of a wrong label at $x$ under $\delta^\star$?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1"}
Given $X = x$, $Y$ is $1$ with probability $p(x)$. If you predict $1$, when is that a mistake, and what does the mistake cost?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2"}
(b) Compare the two expected costs and solve the inequality for $p(x)$. "Not both $0$" is what lets you divide.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 3"}
(c) Condition on $X$ first (the tower property), as in week 2's exercise 1. What do you know about the inner expectation, at every $x$?
:::

::: {.callout-tip .answer collapse="true" title="Reveal solution"}
(a) Predicting $1$ is a mistake when $Y = 0$, which has probability $1 - p(x)$, and then costs $c_{FP}$; predicting $0$ is a mistake when $Y = 1$, probability $p(x)$, cost $c_{FN}$:
$$
\mathbb E[\text{cost} \mid \text{predict } 1,\ X = x] = c_{FP}\,(1 - p(x)), \qquad \mathbb E[\text{cost} \mid \text{predict } 0,\ X = x] = c_{FN}\, p(x).
$$

(b) Predicting $1$ is cheaper when
$$
c_{FN}\,p > c_{FP}\,(1 - p) \iff p\,(c_{FP} + c_{FN}) > c_{FP} \iff p > \frac{c_{FP}}{c_{FP} + c_{FN}},
$$
dividing by $c_{FP} + c_{FN} > 0$. At $p(x) = c^\star$ the two expected costs are equal, so either prediction is optimal.

(c) For any rule $\delta$, by the tower property,
$$
\mathbb E\big[\text{cost}(\delta(X), Y)\big] = \mathbb E_X\Big[\,\mathbb E\big[\text{cost}(\delta(X), Y) \mid X\big]\Big].
$$
At $X = x$ the inner expectation is the expected cost of the prediction $\delta(x)$ from (a), and by (b) it is at least the expected cost of $\delta^\star(x)$. An inequality that holds at every $x$ survives averaging over $X$. $\blacksquare$ This is week 2's step: minimize the expected loss at each $x$, then average.

(d) $c^\star = \tfrac12$: predict the more probable class, the **Bayes classifier**. The probability of a wrong label at $x$ is $1 - p(x)$ if you predict $1$ and $p(x)$ if you predict $0$, so under $\delta^\star$ it is $\min(p(x), 1 - p(x))$. Equal costs make the expected cost a multiple of the probability of error, so by (c) no rule has a smaller overall probability of error.

Common errors: the ratio upside down, $c_{FN}/(c_{FP} + c_{FN})$ (check an extreme: if a miss were infinitely costly the threshold must go to $0$, and only $c_{FP}/(c_{FP} + c_{FN})$ does that); choosing one threshold to minimize the overall cost directly, without the argument at each $x$; reading the theorem as a statement about $\hat p$. It is about the true $p(x)$; with $\hat p$ in its place the rule is a plug-in rule, only as good as the estimate.
:::

**Exercise 2 (confounding gap).** The lecture's DAG made linear. $Z$, $\varepsilon_T$ and $\varepsilon_Y$ are independent, $\varepsilon_T$ and $\varepsilon_Y$ have mean $0$, $\mathrm{Var}(T) > 0$, and
$$
T = \alpha Z + \varepsilon_T, \qquad Y = \tau T + \gamma Z + \varepsilon_Y.
$$

(a) Under $do(T = t)$, which variables keep their values? Show that $\mathbb E[Y \mid do(T = t)] = \tau t + \gamma\, \mathbb E Z$, so that moving $t$ from $0$ to $1$ changes the mean of $Y$ by $\tau$.

(b) As observed, show that $\mathbb E[Y \mid T = t] = \tau t + \gamma\, \mathbb E[Z \mid T = t]$, and hence
$$
\mathbb E[Y \mid T = 1] - \mathbb E[Y \mid T = 0] = \tau + \gamma\,\big(\mathbb E[Z \mid T = 1] - \mathbb E[Z \mid T = 0]\big).
$$
Where did you use independence?

(c) Show that the population slope of the least-squares line of $Y$ on $T$ alone, $\mathrm{Cov}(T, Y)/\mathrm{Var}(T)$, is $\tau + \gamma\,\delta$ with $\delta = \mathrm{Cov}(Z, T)/\mathrm{Var}(T)$. Which quantity in week 2's omitted-variable bias plays the role of $\delta$?

(d) When is the gap zero?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1"}
(a) Delete $T$'s equation and set $T = t$. Is $Z$ upstream or downstream of $T$?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2"}
(b) Take $\mathbb E[\,\cdot \mid T = t]$ of $Y$'s equation term by term. $T$ is a function of $Z$ and $\varepsilon_T$; what does that say about $\varepsilon_Y$ and $T$?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 3"}
(c) Expand $\mathrm{Cov}(T, Y)$ using $Y$'s equation. $\mathrm{Cov}(T, \varepsilon_Y) = 0$ for the reason you found in (b).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .answer collapse="true" title="Reveal solution"}
(a) $Z$ is upstream of $T$ and the noises are their own, so $Z$ and $\varepsilon_Y$ keep their values: $Y = \tau t + \gamma Z + \varepsilon_Y$, and $\mathbb E[Y \mid do(T = t)] = \tau t + \gamma\,\mathbb E Z + 0$. The difference between $t = 1$ and $t = 0$ is $\tau$, the coefficient on $T$ in $Y$'s own equation.

(b) $\mathbb E[Y \mid T = t] = \tau t + \gamma\,\mathbb E[Z \mid T = t] + \mathbb E[\varepsilon_Y \mid T = t]$. $T = \alpha Z + \varepsilon_T$ is a function of $(Z, \varepsilon_T)$, and $\varepsilon_Y$ is independent of $(Z, \varepsilon_T)$, so $\varepsilon_Y$ is independent of $T$ and $\mathbb E[\varepsilon_Y \mid T = t] = \mathbb E\,\varepsilon_Y = 0$. That is where independence is used. Subtracting the expressions at $t = 1$ and $t = 0$ gives the gap. $\blacksquare$

(c) $\mathrm{Cov}(T, Y) = \tau\,\mathrm{Var}(T) + \gamma\,\mathrm{Cov}(T, Z) + \mathrm{Cov}(T, \varepsilon_Y)$, and the last term is $0$. Dividing by $\mathrm{Var}(T)$ gives $\tau + \gamma\,\delta$. Here $\delta$, the population slope of $Z$ on $T$, plays the role of $\hat\delta$ (the slope of the omitted $\mathbf x_2$ on the kept $\mathbf x_1$), $\tau$ plays $\beta_1$ and $\gamma$ plays $\beta_2$: omitted-variable bias, read causally. With these equations $\delta = \alpha\,\mathrm{Var}(Z)/(\alpha^2\,\mathrm{Var}(Z) + \mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon_T))$.

(d) When $\gamma = 0$ ($Z$ does not affect $Y$), or when the mean of $Z$ does not move with $T$; for example $\alpha = 0$, when $T$ does not depend on $Z$ at all, which is what randomizing $T$ arranges. (The gap in (b) compares two conditional means; the slope in (c) is a least-squares slope. They agree, gap $= \gamma\delta$, when $\mathbb E[Z \mid T]$ is linear in $T$, as it is when everything is normal.)

Common errors: letting $Z$ change under the intervention; writing $\mathbb E[\varepsilon_Y \mid T = t] = 0$ without saying why (it needs the independence, which an unobserved common cause of $T$ and $Y$ would break); writing the bias as $\gamma\alpha$ instead of $\gamma\delta$.
:::

**Exercise 3 (adjustment theorem).** The lecture stated this one; prove it. Structural model: $Z$, $\varepsilon_T$ and $\varepsilon_Y$ independent, $T = h(Z, \varepsilon_T)$, $Y = g(T, Z, \varepsilon_Y)$; under $do(T = t)$ the equation for $T$ is deleted, $T$ is set to $t$, and everything else keeps its equation and its noise. Suppose $P(T = t \mid Z) > 0$ with probability one (for a continuous $T$: the conditional density of $T$ at $t$ given $Z$ is positive with probability one). Show that
$$
\mathbb E[Y \mid do(T = t)] = \mathbb E_Z\Big[\,\mathbb E[Y \mid T = t, Z]\,\Big],
$$
and say where each assumption is used: the independence of the noises, $Z$ not being a consequence of $T$, and the condition on $P(T = t \mid Z)$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1"}
Start from the intervened world. What is $Y$ under $do(T = t)$, and which variables keep their values? Give the average over the noise with $Z$ frozen a name: $m_t(z) = \mathbb E\big[g(t, z, \varepsilon_Y)\big]$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2"}
Use the second ST102 fact, with $V = \varepsilon_Y$ and $Z$ in the role of $X$, to show $\mathbb E[Y \mid do(T = t)] = \mathbb E_Z\big[m_t(Z)\big]$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 3"}
Now the observed world: on $\{T = t, Z = z\}$, $Y = g(t, z, \varepsilon_Y)$. Why is $\varepsilon_Y$ independent of $(T, Z)$, and what does that give for $\mathbb E[Y \mid T = t, Z = z]$?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 4"}
Why is the distribution of $Z$ the same in the observed and the intervened worlds?
:::

::: {.callout-tip .answer collapse="true" title="Reveal solution"}
Hint 1: under $do(T = t)$, $Y = g(t, Z, \varepsilon_Y)$, with $Z$ and $\varepsilon_Y$ unchanged ($Z$ is upstream of $T$). Hint 2: $\varepsilon_Y$ is independent of $Z$, so $\mathbb E[g(t, Z, \varepsilon_Y) \mid Z = z] = m_t(z)$, and by the tower property
$$
\mathbb E[Y \mid do(T = t)] = \mathbb E\big[g(t, Z, \varepsilon_Y)\big] = \mathbb E_Z\big[m_t(Z)\big].
$$
Hint 3: $T = h(Z, \varepsilon_T)$ is a function of $(Z, \varepsilon_T)$ and $\varepsilon_Y$ is independent of $(Z, \varepsilon_T)$, so $\varepsilon_Y$ is independent of $(T, Z)$. Wherever $P(T = t \mid Z = z) > 0$, the event $\{T = t, Z = z\}$ can be conditioned on, and on it $Y = g(t, z, \varepsilon_Y)$, so
$$
\mathbb E[Y \mid T = t, Z = z] = \mathbb E\big[g(t, z, \varepsilon_Y) \mid T = t, Z = z\big] = m_t(z).
$$
Hint 4: $Z$ is upstream of $T$, so the intervention does not change it, and its distribution is the same in the two worlds. Averaging the last display over it,
$$
\mathbb E[Y \mid do(T = t)] = \mathbb E_Z\big[m_t(Z)\big] = \mathbb E_Z\Big[\,\mathbb E[Y \mid T = t, Z]\,\Big]. \qquad \blacksquare
$$
Where each assumption is used: the independence of the noises in the observed-world step (a common cause of $T$ and $Y$ left out of $Z$ would sit in both $\varepsilon_T$ and $\varepsilon_Y$, making them dependent); $Z$ not a consequence of $T$ in the intervened-world step (a $Z$ downstream of $T$ would change when $T$ is set, and its distribution would differ between the worlds); $P(T = t \mid Z) > 0$ with probability one, so that $\mathbb E[Y \mid T = t, Z = z]$ is defined for almost every $z$ the average runs over (if it failed on a set of $z$ with positive probability, the right-hand side would not be defined there; for a continuous $T$, read it as the conditional density). If $Z$ is empty, $T = h(\varepsilon_T)$ is independent of $\varepsilon_Y$ and the same lines give $\mathbb E[Y \mid do(T = t)] = \mathbb E[Y \mid T = t]$: randomization.

Common errors: letting $Z$ respond to the intervention; asserting $\mathbb E[Y \mid T = t, Z = z] = m_t(z)$ without the independence of $\varepsilon_Y$ from $(T, Z)$; reading the theorem as "regress $Y$ on $T$ and $Z$ and take the coefficient", which is one way to estimate the inside when the conditional mean is linear, not what the theorem says.
:::

**Exercise 4 (propensity weighting theorem).** The lecture proved this one. Close the slides and prove it again. The structural model of exercise 3, with $T \in \{0, 1\}$ and the propensity score $\pi(z) = P(T = 1 \mid Z = z)$, where $0 < \pi(Z) < 1$ with probability one.

(a) Show that $\mathbb E[Y \mid do(T = 1)] = \mathbb E\big[T\,Y/\pi(Z)\big]$, and say where you used the independence of the noises, $Z$ not being a consequence of $T$, and $\pi(Z) > 0$.

(b) Show that $\mathbb E[Y \mid do(T = 0)] = \mathbb E\big[(1 - T)\,Y/(1 - \pi(Z))\big]$.

(c) Without the structural model, show by conditioning on $Z$ that $\mathbb E\big[T\,Y/\pi(Z)\big] = \mathbb E_Z\big[\,\mathbb E[Y \mid T = 1, Z]\,\big]$. What does that say about the two theorems?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1"}
(a) $T$ is $0$ or $1$. Check that $T\,Y = T\,g(1, Z, \varepsilon_Y)$ in both cases.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2"}
(a) Use the second ST102 fact with $V = \varepsilon_T$ and $(Z, \varepsilon_Y)$ in the role of $X$: what is $\mathbb E[T \mid Z, \varepsilon_Y]$? Then condition on $(Z, \varepsilon_Y)$ with the tower property.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 3"}
(c) $T\,Y = Y\,\mathbb 1[T = 1]$, so $\mathbb E[T\,Y \mid Z] = P(T = 1 \mid Z)\, \mathbb E[Y \mid T = 1, Z]$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .answer collapse="true" title="Reveal solution"}
(a) If $T = 0$ both sides of $T\,Y = T\,g(1, Z, \varepsilon_Y)$ are $0$; if $T = 1$, $Y = g(1, Z, \varepsilon_Y)$. Next, $T = h(Z, \varepsilon_T)$ and $\varepsilon_T$ is independent of $(Z, \varepsilon_Y)$, so by the second ST102 fact $\mathbb E[T \mid Z = z, \varepsilon_Y = e] = P\big(h(z, \varepsilon_T) = 1\big)$. The same fact with $Z$ alone gives $\pi(z) = P\big(h(z, \varepsilon_T) = 1\big)$. So $\mathbb E[T \mid Z, \varepsilon_Y] = \pi(Z)$. Since $g(1, Z, \varepsilon_Y)/\pi(Z)$ is a function of $(Z, \varepsilon_Y)$, and $\pi(Z) > 0$ lets us divide, the tower property gives
$$
\mathbb E\Big[\frac{T\,Y}{\pi(Z)}\Big] = \mathbb E\Big[\,\mathbb E[T \mid Z, \varepsilon_Y]\,\frac{g(1, Z, \varepsilon_Y)}{\pi(Z)}\Big] = \mathbb E\big[g(1, Z, \varepsilon_Y)\big] = \mathbb E[Y \mid do(T = 1)].
$$
The last step: under $do(T = 1)$, $Y = g(1, Z, \varepsilon_Y)$ with $Z$ and $\varepsilon_Y$ unchanged. $\blacksquare$

Where each assumption is used: the independence of $\varepsilon_T$ from $(Z, \varepsilon_Y)$ in $\mathbb E[T \mid Z, \varepsilon_Y] = \pi(Z)$ (a common cause of $T$ and $Y$ left out of $Z$ would sit in both noises, and then $\varepsilon_Y$ would carry information about $T$ beyond $Z$); $\pi(Z) > 0$ to divide; $Z$ not a consequence of $T$ in the last step (a $Z$ downstream of $T$ would change when $T$ is set).

(b) The same lines with $1 - T$ in place of $T$: $(1 - T)\,Y = (1 - T)\,g(0, Z, \varepsilon_Y)$, $\mathbb E[1 - T \mid Z, \varepsilon_Y] = 1 - \pi(Z)$, and $1 - \pi(Z) > 0$ lets us divide.

(c) $\mathbb E[T\,Y \mid Z] = \mathbb E\big[Y\,\mathbb 1[T = 1] \mid Z\big] = \pi(Z)\,\mathbb E[Y \mid T = 1, Z]$. Since $1/\pi(Z)$ is a function of $Z$, the tower property gives
$$
\mathbb E\Big[\frac{T\,Y}{\pi(Z)}\Big] = \mathbb E\Big[\frac{\mathbb E[T\,Y \mid Z]}{\pi(Z)}\Big] = \mathbb E_Z\Big[\,\mathbb E[Y \mid T = 1, Z]\,\Big].
$$
This holds for any joint distribution with $\pi(Z) > 0$: the two theorems have the same right-hand side, written two ways, and the causal assumptions are what make it equal to $\mathbb E[Y \mid do(T = 1)]$. In practice they differ in what you estimate: the adjustment theorem needs a model for $\mathbb E[Y \mid T, Z]$, propensity weighting a model for $\pi(Z)$.

Common errors: writing $\mathbb E[T \mid Z, \varepsilon_Y] = \pi(Z)$ without saying why; weighting by $\pi(Z)$ instead of $1/\pi(Z)$; dropping the $T$ in the numerator, which weights the untreated units too.
:::

## Problems

<!-- About 20 min: problems 1 to 3, pen and paper. Hints are revealed in order after a few minutes, the solution last. -->

**Problem 1 (costs 5 and 1).** A conservation survey classifies penguins from a photograph. Labeling a Chinstrap as an Adelie (a miss) wastes a return visit, cost 5; labeling an Adelie as a Chinstrap (a false alarm) wastes a phone call, cost 1. Write $p(x) = P(\text{Chinstrap} \mid x)$.

(a) Find the threshold on $p(x)$ above which predicting Chinstrap has the smaller expected cost. What happens at the threshold itself?

(b) A fitted model gives $\hat p = 0.25$ for one bird. What does the rule predict, and what would have to be true of $\hat p$ for that prediction to be the best one at that $x$?

(c) The survey hands the same $\hat p$ to two field teams. For team A a miss costs 5 and a false alarm 1; for team B both cost 1. For which values of $\hat p$ do the two teams make different calls?

(d) Say in one sentence what the survey decided when it chose 5 and 1.

::: {.callout-note .answer collapse="true" title="Hint 1"}
(a) Which kind of mistake is the false positive here, and which the false negative? Then exercise 1(b).
:::

::: {.callout-note .answer collapse="true" title="Hint 2"}
(c) Each team has its own threshold. Between the two thresholds, what does each team predict?
:::

::: {.callout-tip .answer collapse="true" title="Reveal answer"}
(a) Predicting Chinstrap is a false alarm when the bird is an Adelie: $c_{FP} = 1$, $c_{FN} = 5$. Expected costs $1 \cdot (1 - p)$ and $5p$, so Chinstrap is cheaper when $p > 1/6 \approx 0.167$. At $p = 1/6$ the two costs are equal and either prediction is optimal.

(b) $\hat p = 0.25 > 1/6$, so the rule says Chinstrap. That is the best decision at $x$ if the true $p(x)$ is at least $1/6$ too: $\hat p$ need not be exact, only on the same side of the threshold as $p(x)$. With an estimate in its place it is a plug-in rule: if the model is badly calibrated there (say the true $p(x)$ is $0.1$) the call is wrong.

(c) Team A's threshold is $1/6$, team B's is $1/2$. For $1/6 < \hat p < 1/2$, A calls Chinstrap and B calls Adelie; at the two end points one team is indifferent. Same model, same bird, different decisions: the difference comes from the costs alone.

(d) That five false alarms are worth one miss: a statement about the survey's resources, not about penguins.

Common errors: swapping the costs (threshold $5/6$); "the model predicts Chinstrap", when the model gives a probability and the rule makes the call.
:::

**Problem 2 (the lecture's DAG, with numbers).** Let $Z$, $\varepsilon_T$ and $\varepsilon_Y$ be independent standard normal variables, $T = Z + \varepsilon_T$ and $Y = T + 2Z + \varepsilon_Y$.

(a) What is the effect on $\mathbb E[Y]$ of raising $t$ by one under $do(T = t)$?

(b) Compute $\mathrm{Var}(T)$, $\mathrm{Cov}(T, Y)$ and the population slope of the regression of $Y$ on $T$ alone. Write it as "effect plus gap" and identify the gap.

(c) Compute $\mathbb E[Y \mid T = t, Z = z]$, average it over $Z$, and check that you recover (a). Where did you use that the noises are independent?

::: {.callout-note .answer collapse="true" title="Hint 1"}
(a) and (b) are exercise 2 with $\alpha = \tau = 1$ and $\gamma = 2$. For the covariance, $\mathrm{Cov}(T, Z) = \mathrm{Var}(Z)$ here.
:::

::: {.callout-note .answer collapse="true" title="Hint 2"}
(c) Take $\mathbb E[\,\cdot \mid T = t, Z = z]$ of $Y$'s equation, then exercise 3.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .answer collapse="true" title="Reveal answer"}
(a) Under $do(T = t)$, $Y = t + 2Z + \varepsilon_Y$, so $\mathbb E[Y \mid do(T = t)] = t$ and raising $t$ by one raises it by $1$.

(b) $\mathrm{Var}(T) = 1 + 1 = 2$. $\mathrm{Cov}(T, Y) = \mathrm{Var}(T) + 2\,\mathrm{Cov}(T, Z) + \mathrm{Cov}(T, \varepsilon_Y) = 2 + 2 + 0 = 4$. Slope $4/2 = 2 = 1 + 2 \cdot \tfrac12$: the effect $\tau = 1$ plus the gap $\gamma\delta = 2 \cdot \tfrac12$, with $\delta = \mathrm{Cov}(Z, T)/\mathrm{Var}(T) = \tfrac12$. The naive slope credits $T$ with what $Z$ contributes through selection, and here the gap is as large as the effect.

(c) $\mathbb E[Y \mid T = t, Z = z] = t + 2z + \mathbb E[\varepsilon_Y \mid T = t, Z = z] = t + 2z$, because $\varepsilon_Y$ is independent of $(Z, \varepsilon_T)$ and so of $(T, Z)$. Averaging over $Z$: $\mathbb E_Z[t + 2Z] = t$, which is (a). The independence is what made $\mathbb E[\varepsilon_Y \mid T = t, Z = z]$ zero. Normality is what makes this work at every $t$: given $Z$, $T$ has a positive density everywhere, so the adjustment theorem's condition holds.

Common errors: in (a), letting $Z$ change when $T$ is set; in (b), $\mathrm{Cov}(T, Z) = 0$.
:::

**Problem 3 (propensity weighting by hand).** $Z$ is $0$ or $1$, each with probability $\tfrac12$. Treatment depends on $Z$: $T = h(Z, \varepsilon_T)$ with $\pi(0) = 0.2$ and $\pi(1) = 0.8$. The outcome is $Y = 2T + 4Z + \varepsilon_Y$, with $\varepsilon_Y$ of mean $0$, and $Z$, $\varepsilon_T$, $\varepsilon_Y$ independent.

(a) What is $\mathbb E[Y \mid do(T = 1)] - \mathbb E[Y \mid do(T = 0)]$?

(b) Picture 100 units in exactly these proportions. How many are treated with $Z = 0$, treated with $Z = 1$, untreated with $Z = 0$, untreated with $Z = 1$? Compute $\mathbb E[Y \mid T = 1] - \mathbb E[Y \mid T = 0]$ and write it as effect plus gap.

(c) Give each treated unit the weight $1/\pi(Z)$ and each untreated unit the weight $1/(1 - \pi(Z))$, and multiply each count from (b) by its weight. What do the weighted treated units look like? Compute $\mathbb E\big[T\,Y/\pi(Z)\big]$ and $\mathbb E\big[(1 - T)\,Y/(1 - \pi(Z))\big]$ and compare with (a).

(d) Which units get the largest weights? What would happen to them if $\pi(0)$ were $0.01$?

::: {.callout-note .answer collapse="true" title="Hint 1"}
(a) Under $do(T = t)$, $Z$ keeps its distribution. (b) 50 units have $Z = 0$, and 20 percent of them are treated. Among the treated, what fraction has $Z = 1$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .answer collapse="true" title="Hint 2"}
(c) In the 100 units, $\mathbb E\big[T\,Y/\pi(Z)\big]$ is $\tfrac{1}{100}$ times the sum of $Y/\pi(Z)$ over the treated units. Group them by $Z$: within a group, $Y$ averages $\mathbb E[Y \mid T = 1, Z = z] = 2 + 4z$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .answer collapse="true" title="Reveal answer"}
(a) Under $do(T = t)$, $Y = 2t + 4Z + \varepsilon_Y$, so $\mathbb E[Y \mid do(T = t)] = 2t + 4 \cdot \tfrac12 = 2t + 2$: $4$ and $2$, effect $2$.

(b) Of the 50 units with $Z = 0$, 10 are treated and 40 are not; of the 50 with $Z = 1$, 40 are treated and 10 are not. So $\mathbb E[Z \mid T = 1] = 40/50 = 0.8$ and $\mathbb E[Z \mid T = 0] = 0.2$, and $\mathbb E[Y \mid T = 1] = 2 + 4 \cdot 0.8 = 5.2$, $\mathbb E[Y \mid T = 0] = 4 \cdot 0.2 = 0.8$. The naive difference is $4.4 = 2 + 4\,(0.8 - 0.2)$: the effect $2$ plus a gap of $2.4$. This is the lecture's confounding gap; its derivation (exercise 2(b)) used only $Y$'s equation and the independence of $\varepsilon_Y$, not the linear equation for $T$.

(c) Treated: 10 units with $Z = 0$ at weight $1/0.2 = 5$ count as 50; 40 units with $Z = 1$ at weight $1/0.8 = 1.25$ count as 50. The weighted treated units have the whole population's $Z$: half $0$, half $1$. The untreated are the same: $40 \cdot 1.25 = 50$ and $10 \cdot 5 = 50$. Then
$$
\mathbb E\Big[\frac{T\,Y}{\pi(Z)}\Big] = \frac{10 \cdot 5 \cdot 2 + 40 \cdot 1.25 \cdot 6}{100} = 4, \qquad \mathbb E\Big[\frac{(1 - T)\,Y}{1 - \pi(Z)}\Big] = \frac{40 \cdot 1.25 \cdot 0 + 10 \cdot 5 \cdot 4}{100} = 2,
$$
which are $\mathbb E[Y \mid do(T = 1)]$ and $\mathbb E[Y \mid do(T = 0)]$ from (a). Difference $2$.

(d) The treated units with $Z = 0$ and the untreated units with $Z = 1$: the units whose treatment was unlikely given their $Z$. Each stands in for the many units like it that went the other way. With $\pi(0) = 0.01$, about one in a hundred units with $Z = 0$ is treated, and each gets weight $100$. The condition $\pi(Z) > 0$ still holds, but in a sample of a few hundred units one or two treated units with $Z = 0$ would carry the estimate for half the population, so it would be unstable.

Common errors: weighting by $\pi(Z)$ instead of $1/\pi(Z)$; weighting the untreated by $1/\pi(Z)$ instead of $1/(1 - \pi(Z))$; dividing by the 50 treated units instead of all 100.
:::

### Optional, can be done at home

<!-- Not in the seminar. Hints are in the student file. -->

**Problem 4 (the causation runs the other way).** $Y = \varepsilon_Y$ with variance $4$, and $T = 0.4\,Y + \varepsilon_T$, with $\varepsilon_T$ of variance $0.16$, independent of $Y$. Find the population slope of $Y$ on $T$ and the effect of raising $t$ by one. Compare with problem 2(b).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1"}
$\mathrm{Var}(T) = 0.4^2\,\mathrm{Var}(Y) + \mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon_T)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .answer collapse="true" title="Reveal answer"}
$\mathrm{Var}(T) = 0.16 \cdot 4 + 0.16 = 0.8$, $\mathrm{Cov}(T, Y) = 0.4 \cdot 4 = 1.6$, slope $2$. The effect is $0$: $Y$'s equation has no $T$ in it, and setting $T$ changes nothing upstream. The same population slope as problem 2(b), and as a world with $Y = 2T + \varepsilon$: the regression alone cannot tell the three apart.

Common errors: "the slope is 2, so the effect is 2".
:::

**Problem 5 (a model that predicts well).** A hospital fits a model that predicts which patients will be readmitted within 30 days, and it predicts well on held-out patients. Management proposes to reduce readmissions by acting on the model's strongest predictor. Draw the DAGs of three worlds consistent with that held-out score, say in which of them the plan works, and say what the score told you about which world you are in.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1"}
The lecture's explanations of an observed correlation: the predictor causes readmission, a common cause drives both, or readmission risk drives the predictor.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .answer collapse="true" title="Reveal answer"}
A: the predictor causes readmission (for example, discharge before a test result is back); acting on it can work. B: a common cause such as severity drives both; acting on the predictor changes nothing. C: readmission risk drives the predictor (for example, patients at high risk are put on extra monitoring, and the monitoring is the predictor); acting on it changes nothing. The held-out score is the same in all three, so it told you nothing about which world you are in. Deciding needs knowledge of the mechanism, or an experiment.

Common errors: "the model is accurate, so the predictor is a cause"; drawing world C with the arrow the wrong way round.
:::

### 1. Penguins: a probability and a threshold

<!-- 18 min: steps 1 to 5, questions 1 to 3. -->

Adelie against Chinstrap, from the bill. Keep the two species and the birds with complete measurements.

```{r}
pg <- palmerpenguins::penguins |>   # modeldata also has a penguins; be explicit
  filter(species != "Gentoo") |>
  drop_na(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm, flipper_length_mm) |>
  mutate(chinstrap = as.numeric(species == "Chinstrap"))
ggplot(pg, aes(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm, colour = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(end = 0.7)
```

**Step 1.** How many birds, and what proportion are Chinstraps? What accuracy would a classifier that always predicts the more common species achieve?

```{r}
#| eval: false
# nrow(pg); mean(pg$____)
# max(____, 1 - ____)
# ...
```

::: {.callout-tip .answer collapse="true" title="Reveal solution"}
```{r}
nrow(pg)
mean(pg$chinstrap)
max(mean(pg$chinstrap), 1 - mean(pg$chinstrap))
```
:::

**Step 2.** Fit the logistic regression of `chinstrap` on the two bill measurements with `glm(..., family = binomial)`. Look at `tidy()`, then at `tidy(..., exponentiate = TRUE)`.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# fit_bill <- glm(____ ~ ____ + ____, family = binomial, data = pg)
# tidy(fit_bill)
# tidy(fit_bill, exponentiate = TRUE)
# ...
```

::: {.callout-tip .answer collapse="true" title="Reveal solution"}
```{r}
fit_bill <- glm(chinstrap ~ bill_length_mm + bill_depth_mm, family = binomial, data = pg)
tidy(fit_bill)
tidy(fit_bill, exponentiate = TRUE)
```
:::

Checkpoint (run it; if it stops, fix step 2 before going on):

```{r}
#| eval: !expr exists("fit_bill")
stopifnot(inherits(fit_bill, "glm"), length(coef(fit_bill)) == 3,
          all(fitted(fit_bill) >= 0 & fitted(fit_bill) <= 1))
```

You may have seen a warning that fitted probabilities are numerically 0 or 1: the two species are nearly separable on these two measurements (step 3 counts the errors). This is the lecture's "Challenges" slide in real life; next week says what it does to the fitting.

**Question 1.** Read the exponentiated coefficient on `bill_length_mm`. What happens to the odds of Chinstrap when bill length increases by one millimeter and bill depth is held fixed? Is that the change in the probability? Is it what would happen to a bird whose bill grew by a millimeter?

::: {.callout-tip .answer collapse="true" title="Reveal answer"}
The odds of Chinstrap are multiplied by about $e^{2.20} \approx 9.0$ per millimeter, with bill depth held fixed. That is a multiplier on the odds $p/(1 - p)$, not a change in $p$: how much $p$ moves depends on where it starts (near $0$ or $1$ a ninefold change in the odds moves $p$ very little; near $\tfrac12$ it moves it a lot). The standard error is large ($0.69$ on the log-odds scale, so the interval for the multiplier runs from about $2$ to about $35$), because the classes are nearly separable. And "holding depth fixed" is the lecture's ceteris paribus: a comparison between birds in the fitted model, not what would happen to one bird if its bill grew. Nothing here is causal.
:::

**Step 3.** The confusion matrix at threshold $\tfrac12$, with `table()`. From it, compute the accuracy, the true positive rate and the false positive rate.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# p_hat <- fitted(fit_bill)
# tab <- table(truth = pg$chinstrap, predicted = as.numeric(p_hat > ____))
# tab
# accuracy <- (tab[1, 1] + tab[2, 2]) / sum(tab)
# tpr <- ____ ; fpr <- ____
# ...
```

::: {.callout-tip .answer collapse="true" title="Reveal solution"}
```{r}
p_hat <- fitted(fit_bill)
tab <- table(truth = pg$chinstrap, predicted = as.numeric(p_hat > 0.5))
tab
accuracy <- (tab[1, 1] + tab[2, 2]) / sum(tab)
tpr <- tab[2, 2] / sum(tab[2, ])
fpr <- tab[1, 2] / sum(tab[1, ])
c(accuracy = accuracy, tpr = tpr, fpr = fpr)
```
:::

Checkpoint:

```{r}
#| eval: !expr exists("tpr") && exists("fpr")
stopifnot(sum(tab) == nrow(pg), tpr >= 0, tpr <= 1, fpr >= 0, fpr <= 1)
```

**Step 4.** The bill model is nearly perfect, so it cannot show the trade-off. Fit a weaker model on `flipper_length_mm` alone, then compute the ROC curve *yourself*: at every threshold where it can change (0, then each distinct fitted probability), the true positive rate and the false positive rate. Plot one against the other. The loop is set up; you write the two rates.

```{r}
#| eval: false
fit_flipper <- glm(chinstrap ~ flipper_length_mm, family = binomial, data = pg)
pg <- pg |> mutate(p_flipper = fitted(fit_flipper))
thresholds <- c(0, sort(unique(pg$p_flipper)))   # 0, then every distinct fitted probability
roc_by_hand <- map_dfr(thresholds, function(t) {
  yhat <- as.numeric(pg$p_flipper > t)
  # tibble(t = t,
  #        tpr = sum(yhat == 1 & pg$chinstrap == 1) / sum(____),
  #        fpr = sum(____) / sum(____))
  # ...
})
# ggplot(roc_by_hand, aes(____, ____)) + geom_path() + coord_equal()
# ...
```

::: {.callout-tip .answer collapse="true" title="Reveal solution"}
```{r}
fit_flipper <- glm(chinstrap ~ flipper_length_mm, family = binomial, data = pg)
pg <- pg |> mutate(p_flipper = fitted(fit_flipper))
thresholds <- c(0, sort(unique(pg$p_flipper)))   # 0, then every distinct fitted probability
roc_by_hand <- map_dfr(thresholds, function(t) {
  yhat <- as.numeric(pg$p_flipper > t)
  tibble(t = t,
         tpr = sum(yhat == 1 & pg$chinstrap == 1) / sum(pg$chinstrap == 1),
         fpr = sum(yhat == 1 & pg$chinstrap == 0) / sum(pg$chinstrap == 0))
})
ggplot(roc_by_hand, aes(fpr, tpr)) +
  geom_path() +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dotted") +
  coord_equal()
```
:::

Checkpoint:

```{r}
#| eval: !expr exists("roc_by_hand")
stopifnot(nrow(roc_by_hand) == length(thresholds),
          all(roc_by_hand$tpr >= 0 & roc_by_hand$tpr <= 1),
          roc_by_hand$tpr[1] == 1, roc_by_hand$fpr[1] == 1)
```

**Question 2.** The area under your curve equals the probability that a randomly chosen Chinstrap gets a higher fitted probability than a randomly chosen Adelie, with a tie counting half. Why does accumulating one point per threshold produce that probability? Why are ties certain to occur with this model?

::: {.callout-tip .answer collapse="true" title="Reveal answer"}
Moving the threshold down past one bird's score adds that bird to the predicted Chinstraps: a Chinstrap raises the TPR by $1/n_1$, an Adelie raises the FPR by $1/n_0$. The area under the path therefore adds up, for each Adelie step to the right, the height of the curve there, which is the fraction of Chinstraps already passed, those scoring above that Adelie. Summing over Adelies and dividing by $n_0$ gives the fraction of (Chinstrap, Adelie) pairs in which the Chinstrap scores higher; a tie is a diagonal step and contributes half. Ties are certain because `flipper_length_mm` is recorded in whole millimeters and $\hat p$ is a monotone function of it, so birds with the same flipper length have the same score; about 4 percent of the Chinstrap and Adelie pairs tie. By hand:

```{r}
p1 <- pg$p_flipper[pg$chinstrap == 1]
p0 <- pg$p_flipper[pg$chinstrap == 0]
mean(outer(p1, p0, ">") + 0.5 * outer(p1, p0, "=="))
```

The area under your curve, by the trapezoid rule (a tie is a diagonal step, so it counts half), is the same number:

```{r}
r <- arrange(roc_by_hand, fpr, tpr)
sum(diff(r$fpr) * (head(r$tpr, -1) + tail(r$tpr, -1)) / 2)
```
:::

**Step 5.** Costs. A miss costs 5, a false alarm 1. For each threshold on a grid from 0 to 1 in steps of 0.01, compute the cost per bird on the 219 birds, $5 \cdot (\text{misses}/n) + 1 \cdot (\text{false alarms}/n)$, find the threshold that minimizes it, and compare with problem 1's threshold.

```{r}
#| eval: false
grid <- seq(0, 1, by = 0.01)
# costs <- map_dfr(grid, function(t) {
#   yhat <- as.numeric(pg$p_flipper > t)
#   tibble(t = t, cost = (5 * sum(____) + 1 * sum(____)) / nrow(pg))
# })
# ggplot(costs, aes(t, cost)) + geom_line()
# costs |> slice_min(cost, n = 3)
# ...
```

::: {.callout-tip .answer collapse="true" title="Reveal solution"}
```{r}
grid <- seq(0, 1, by = 0.01)
costs <- map_dfr(grid, function(t) {
  yhat <- as.numeric(pg$p_flipper > t)
  tibble(t = t,
         cost = (5 * sum(yhat == 0 & pg$chinstrap == 1) + 1 * sum(yhat == 1 & pg$chinstrap == 0)) / nrow(pg))
})
ggplot(costs, aes(t, cost)) + geom_line()
costs |> slice_min(cost, n = 3)
c(formula = 1 / (1 + 5))
```
:::

Checkpoint:

```{r}
#| eval: !expr exists("costs")
stopifnot(nrow(costs) == length(grid), all(costs$cost >= 0))
```

**Question 3.** The cost-minimizing threshold is well below $\tfrac12$, and the classifier now raises many false alarms. Who decided that, and in what sense is this classifier "better" than the one at $\tfrac12$? Is the number you found the population optimum?

::: {.callout-tip .answer collapse="true" title="Reveal answer"}
The survey did, by choosing costs 5 and 1; the model contributed only $\hat p$. On these 219 birds it has a lower cost per bird under those costs, and a lower accuracy: "better" has no meaning until a loss is chosen. The formula gives the population optimum for the true $p(x)$; the curve is an empirical cost on the birds the model was fitted to, with $\hat p$ plugged in, and its minimum is flat (several thresholds near $1/6$ tie). So the agreement is between an estimate and the formula, not a proof that the formula is right for new birds. That evaluating on the training rows flatters the model is the validation week's subject.
:::

### 2. Simulated worlds: adjustment and propensity weighting

<!-- 22 min: steps 1 to 4, questions 4 to 6. -->

Four simulated worlds in which $Y$ is regressed on $X$. In the lecture the target variable was called $T$; here it is `X`, because `T` is `TRUE` in R. The function draws the noise once and keeps it, so that an intervention can be computed for the *same* units. World D is the lecture's DAG with the confounder $Z$ observed: $Z \to X$, $Z \to Y$, $X \to Y$. Step 4 adds a fifth world, E, with the same DAG and a binary treatment.

```{r}
simulate_world <- function(world, n = 500) {
  e_u <- rnorm(n)
  e_x <- rnorm(n)
  e_y <- rnorm(n)
  if (world == "A") {           # X causes Y
    X <- e_x
    Y <- 2 * X + e_y
    Z <- NA
  } else if (world == "B") {    # U causes both; U is not observed
    U <- e_u
    X <- U + 0.5 * e_x
    Y <- 2.5 * U + e_y
    Z <- NA
  } else if (world == "C") {    # Y causes X
    Y <- 2 * e_y
    X <- 0.4 * Y + 0.4 * e_x
    Z <- NA
  } else {                      # D: Z causes both, and X causes Y; Z is observed
    Z <- e_u
    X <- 5 - 2 * Z + e_x
    Y <- 4 + 2 * Z - 3 * X + e_y
  }
  tibble(world = world, X = X, Y = Y, Z = Z, e_u = e_u, e_x = e_x, e_y = e_y)
}
worlds <- bind_rows(simulate_world("A"), simulate_world("B"), simulate_world("C"), simulate_world("D"))
```

**Step 1.** In each world, fit `lm(Y ~ X)` and report the slope.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# worlds |>
#   group_by(world) |>
#   summarise(slope = coef(lm(____))[2])
# ...
```

::: {.callout-tip .answer collapse="true" title="Reveal solution"}
```{r}
worlds |>
  group_by(world) |>
  summarise(slope = coef(lm(Y ~ X))[2])
```
:::

**Question 4.** Before you intervene: for each world, write down what you expect to happen to $Y$ when $X$ is set to $X + 1$ for every unit with the same noise, and the average change. Use each world's equations, and exercise 2 for world D.

::: {.callout-tip .answer collapse="true" title="Reveal answer"}
A: $Y$ rises by exactly $2$ for every unit (its equation has $2X$). B: nothing; $Y$ depends on $U$ and its own noise only. C: nothing; $Y$ is upstream of $X$. D: $Y$ falls by exactly $3$ for every unit, the coefficient on $X$ in $Y$'s equation, while the slope in step 1 is about $-3.8$: $\mathrm{Cov}(X, Y)/\mathrm{Var}(X) = (2 \cdot (-2) - 3 \cdot 5)/5 = -19/5$, the effect $-3$ plus the confounding gap $2 \cdot (-2/5)$.
:::

**Step 2.** Now intervene: set $X$ to $X + 1$ for every unit and recompute $Y$ **with the same noise**, following each world's equations. Write the four `Y_do` lines and compute the average change in $Y$ in each world.

```{r}
#| eval: false
intervene <- function(d) {
  d |> mutate(
    X_do = X + 1,
    # Y_do = case_when(
    #   world == "A" ~ ____,
    #   world == "B" ~ ____,
    #   world == "C" ~ ____,
    #   world == "D" ~ ____
    # )
    # ...
  )
}
worlds_do <- intervene(worlds)
worlds_do |>
  group_by(world) |>
  summarise(slope = coef(lm(Y ~ X))[2],
            effect_of_intervention = mean(Y_do - Y))
```

::: {.callout-tip .answer collapse="true" title="Reveal solution"}
```{r}
intervene <- function(d) {
  d |> mutate(
    X_do = X + 1,
    Y_do = case_when(
      world == "A" ~ 2 * X_do + e_y,
      world == "B" ~ 2.5 * e_u + e_y,
      world == "C" ~ Y,
      world == "D" ~ 4 + 2 * Z - 3 * X_do + e_y
    )
  )
}
worlds_do <- intervene(worlds)
worlds_do |>
  group_by(world) |>
  summarise(slope = coef(lm(Y ~ X))[2],
            effect_of_intervention = mean(Y_do - Y))
```

The average change is the average effect of shifting every unit's $X$ up by one, computed on these units: exactly $2$, $0$, $0$ and $-3$. Each world's equations give every unit the same change, and because the noise is reused nothing else moves.
:::

Checkpoint:

```{r}
#| eval: !expr exists("worlds_do")
stopifnot(all(c("X_do", "Y_do") %in% names(worlds_do)), !anyNA(worlds_do$Y_do))
```

Compare the average changes with your predictions in question 4.

**Step 3.** World D, the adjustment theorem in code. Regress `Y` on `X` and `Z` and read off the coefficient on `X`. Then do what the theorem says: fit $\hat m(x, z)$ for $\mathbb E[Y \mid X = x, Z = z]$ (the same regression), evaluate it at every unit's $Z$ with $X$ set to $X + 1$ and to $X$, and average the difference.

```{r}
#| eval: false
d <- worlds |> filter(world == "D")
# fit_d <- lm(Y ~ ____ + ____, data = d)
# tidy(fit_d)
# mean(predict(fit_d, newdata = mutate(d, X = ____))) - mean(predict(fit_d, newdata = d))
# ...
```

::: {.callout-tip .answer collapse="true" title="Reveal solution"}
```{r}
d <- worlds |> filter(world == "D")
fit_d <- lm(Y ~ X + Z, data = d)
tidy(fit_d)
mean(predict(fit_d, newdata = mutate(d, X = X + 1))) - mean(predict(fit_d, newdata = d))
```
:::

**Question 5.** Compare the coefficient on `X` with the averaged difference, and both with the effect you found in step 2. Which result says the coefficient estimates the effect, which says the averaged difference does, and what about world D made both work? What would go wrong in world B, where the confounder `e_u` is in the table but would not be observed in practice?

::: {.callout-tip .answer collapse="true" title="Reveal answer"}
The two numbers are equal, and both are near $-3$. The coefficient: the partialling-out theorem (week 2) says the coefficient on `X` in the long regression is the slope of `Y` on what is left of `X` after `Z`; in world D what is left is `e_x`, which is independent of everything else in `Y`, so the population value is $-3$ and the sample coefficient estimates it. The averaged difference: the adjustment theorem, $\mathbb E[Y \mid do(X = x)] = \mathbb E_Z[\mathbb E[Y \mid X = x, Z]]$, with the regression as the estimate of the inside. (Step 3 shifts each unit's own `X` rather than setting every unit to one value $x$; in world D the two agree because the effect is the same at every $x$.) The two numbers coincide exactly because the fitted model is linear in `X`, so every unit's difference is the coefficient. Both work because `Z` holds the only common cause of `X` and `Y`, is not a consequence of `X`, and the noises are independent. In world B the common cause is `U`, which you would not have: regress `Y` on `X` alone and you get the slope of about $2$ from step 1, while the effect is $0$. With `e_u` in the regression the coefficient on `X` is about $0$: the theorem working, on a variable you have only because you simulated the world.
:::

**Step 4.** World E: the same DAG, with a binary treatment. Each unit is treated (`X = 1`) with probability $\pi(Z)$, where $\pi(z) = 1/(1 + e^{-(-0.5 + 1.5 z)})$, and $Y = 1 + 2X + 3Z + \varepsilon_Y$, so the effect of treatment is $2$. Compute three estimates of it: the naive difference in means between treated and untreated; the propensity weighting estimate, with $\hat\pi$ from the logistic regression of `X` on `Z`; and the coefficient on `X` in `lm(Y ~ X + Z)`. Then look at the five units with the largest weights.

```{r}
simulate_world_e <- function(n = 2000) {
  Z <- rnorm(n)
  e_x <- runif(n)
  e_y <- rnorm(n)
  X <- as.numeric(e_x < plogis(-0.5 + 1.5 * Z))   # treated with probability pi(Z)
  Y <- 1 + 2 * X + 3 * Z + e_y
  tibble(X = X, Y = Y, Z = Z)
}
d_e <- simulate_world_e()
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
# fit_pi <- glm(____ ~ ____, family = binomial, data = d_e)
# d_e <- d_e |> mutate(pi_hat = fitted(fit_pi),
#                      w = ifelse(X == 1, ____, ____))
# c(naive = mean(d_e$Y[d_e$X == 1]) - mean(d_e$Y[d_e$X == 0]),
#   weighting = mean(d_e$X * d_e$Y / d_e$pi_hat) - mean(____),
#   regression = coef(lm(Y ~ X + Z, data = d_e))[["X"]])
# d_e |> slice_max(w, n = 5)
# ...
```

::: {.callout-tip .answer collapse="true" title="Reveal solution"}
```{r}
fit_pi <- glm(X ~ Z, family = binomial, data = d_e)
d_e <- d_e |> mutate(pi_hat = fitted(fit_pi),
                     w = ifelse(X == 1, 1 / pi_hat, 1 / (1 - pi_hat)))
c(naive = mean(d_e$Y[d_e$X == 1]) - mean(d_e$Y[d_e$X == 0]),
  weighting = mean(d_e$X * d_e$Y / d_e$pi_hat) - mean((1 - d_e$X) * d_e$Y / (1 - d_e$pi_hat)),
  regression = coef(lm(Y ~ X + Z, data = d_e))[["X"]])
d_e |> slice_max(w, n = 5)
```
:::

Checkpoint, then a diagnostic. As in problem 3(c), the weighted treated units and the weighted untreated units should each count as about the whole sample, so both numbers printed should be near 1; a few large weights can move them.

```{r}
#| eval: !expr exists("fit_pi")
stopifnot(all(d_e$pi_hat > 0 & d_e$pi_hat < 1), all(d_e$w >= 1))
c(treated = sum(d_e$w[d_e$X == 1]), untreated = sum(d_e$w[d_e$X == 0])) / nrow(d_e)
```

**Question 6.** Which of the three estimates are near $2$, and which result explains each one? Which units have the largest weights, and what is unusual about them? If the unit with the largest weight had not been in the sample, and the other weights stayed as they are, by how much would the weighting estimate move?

::: {.callout-tip .answer collapse="true" title="Reveal answer"}
The naive difference is about $5.2$: the treated have higher $Z$, and the confounding gap is $3\,(\mathbb E[Z \mid X = 1] - \mathbb E[Z \mid X = 0]) \approx 3 \cdot 1.07$. The weighting estimate is near $2$ by the propensity weighting theorem, with $\hat\pi$ in place of $\pi$; the logistic model for $\pi$ is the right one here, because `X` was generated from a logistic function of `Z`. The regression coefficient is near $2$ by the adjustment theorem (or the partialling-out theorem), because $\mathbb E[Y \mid X, Z]$ is linear in `X` and `Z`. Weighting needs a correct model for the treatment; regression adjustment needs a correct model for the outcome; both need `Z` to hold the common causes. Of the three, the weighting estimate varies most from student to student.

The largest weights belong to treated units with low `Z` or untreated units with high `Z`: units whose treatment was unlikely given their `Z`. Their $\hat\pi$ (or $1 - \hat\pi$) is a few percent, so each stands in for tens of units. The largest weight is usually between about 15 and 100, and it changes a lot from run to run. With the other weights held fixed (not refitting $\hat\pi$), a treated unit with weight $w$ and outcome $Y$ contributes $wY/n$ to the estimate, so leaving it out moves the estimate by about that much: with $w = 50$, $Y = -4$ and $n = 2000$, by $0.1$, from one unit out of 2000.
:::

#### Optional, can be done at home: same noise or fresh noise

**Question 7.** Redraw the noise in `intervene()` (replace `e_y` by `rnorm(n())`) and look at `Y_do - Y` unit by unit in world A. What changes, and what does not? Which version is the counterfactual for a unit, and which is a new draw from the intervened world?

::: {.callout-tip .answer collapse="true" title="Reveal answer"}
With the same noise every unit's change is exactly $2$ in world A; with fresh noise the unit-level differences scatter (variance $2$) while the average stays about $2$. The first is the unit's counterfactual: what would have happened to *this* unit. The second is a draw from the distribution after the intervention. Both have the same average effect; only the first answers "what if" for an individual, and in real data it is never observed, which is one reason causal inference is hard.
:::

#### Optional, can be done at home: weighting against regression, many times

**Question 8.** Simulate world E 200 times and compute the weighting estimate and the regression coefficient each time. Compare their means and their standard deviations. Why is one more variable than the other, and when would you use weighting anyway?

```{r}
#| eval: false
# one_run <- function() {
#   d <- simulate_world_e()
#   pi_hat <- fitted(glm(X ~ Z, family = binomial, data = d))
#   tibble(weighting = ____, regression = ____)
# }
# runs <- map_dfr(1:200, \(i) one_run())
# runs |> summarise(across(everything(), list(mean = mean, sd = sd)))
# ...
```

::: {.callout-tip .answer collapse="true" title="Reveal solution"}
```{r}
one_run <- function() {
  d <- simulate_world_e()
  pi_hat <- fitted(glm(X ~ Z, family = binomial, data = d))
  tibble(weighting = mean(d$X * d$Y / pi_hat) - mean((1 - d$X) * d$Y / (1 - pi_hat)),
         regression = coef(lm(Y ~ X + Z, data = d))[["X"]])
}
runs <- map_dfr(1:200, \(i) one_run())
runs |> summarise(across(everything(), list(mean = mean, sd = sd)))
```

Both average close to $2$. The weighting estimate's standard deviation is three to four times the regression's (about $0.2$ against $0.05$). The regression uses a correct model for $Y$, which here is linear with little noise; weighting ignores what is known about $Y$ and depends on the few units with large weights. Weighting is the choice when you trust a model for who gets treated more than a model for the outcome: for example, when the treatment was assigned by a rule you know.
:::

### Optional, can be done at home: another dataset

**Attrition** (`modeldata::attrition`; **fictional**, made up by IBM data scientists, used only as an exercise): whether an employee leaves, with a threshold-and-costs story (a missed leaver costs a replacement, a false alarm costs a conversation). Leavers are 16 percent, so the accuracy-against-cost point is sharper: at threshold $\tfrac12$ almost nobody is predicted to leave.

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(modeldata)
data(attrition)
att <- attrition |> mutate(left = as.numeric(Attrition == "Yes"))
fit_att <- glm(left ~ OverTime + MonthlyIncome + Age + JobSatisfaction, family = binomial, data = att)
# then steps 3, 4 and 5 with p = fitted(fit_att), costs 10 (a missed leaver) and 1 (a false alarm)
# ...
```
